Dalton Trumbo was a Hollywood screenwriter and University of Colorado Boulder alumnus who attended CU for two years before leaving to pursue his writing career. He became one of Hollywood's most celebrated screenwriters, known for films such as Spartacus, Roman Holiday, and Exodus. During the anti-communist hysteria of the late 1940s, Trumbo was called before the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) in October 1947. Rather than name names or take the Fifth Amendment, Trumbo and nine other film industry workers — known as the Hollywood Ten — refused to cooperate, invoking the First Amendment. They were sentenced to prison for contempt of Congress and subsequently blacklisted from Hollywood. Trumbo continued writing in secret under pseudonyms. The blacklist was effectively broken in 1960 when actor and director Kirk Douglas publicly credited Trumbo by name for writing the screenplay to Spartacus. In the early 1990s, CU Boulder graduate student Kristina Baumli and fellow student Lewis Cardinal organized a campaign to honor Trumbo on campus, noting that almost nobody knew he had attended CU. With endorsements from Kirk Douglas, Robert Redford, Dustin Hoffman, and Katharine Hepburn, the group persuaded the Board of Regents to rename the fountain outside the University Memorial Center in his honor. On October 17, 1993, the fountain was officially rededicated as the Dalton Trumbo Fountain Court. Kirk Douglas, screenwriters Ring Lardner Jr. and Paul Jarrico, and members of the Trumbo family attended the ceremony. The fountain is located outside the University Memorial Center on Norlin Quadrangle and remains a designated free speech and free expression space. Student groups regularly gather there to organize, protest, and engage with the broader community. The space symbolizes Trumbo's legacy as a First Amendment champion. The Keller Center for the Study of the First Amendment at CU Boulder also cites Trumbo as an inspiration for its work on First Amendment rights and liberties.
